subject: humanities
notes: Hangul, the Korean writing system, was created under the direction of King Sejong and announced in 1446.
Sejong wanted ordinary Koreans, who could rarely learn the difficult Chinese characters then used for writing, to be able to read and write.
The Cherokee syllabary was created by Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith, and completed around 1821.
Sequoyah wanted Cherokee people to be able to read and write their own language.
Hangul symbols stand for single sounds, while Cherokee symbols stand for whole syllables.
stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Hangul and the Cherokee syllabary. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Hangul symbols stand for single sounds, while the symbols of the Cherokee syllabary stand for whole syllables.
choices.B: Hangul and the Cherokee syllabary were both created to help people read and write their own language.
choices.C: Hangul was announced in 1446, nearly four centuries before Sequoyah completed the Cherokee syllabary.
choices.D: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith, completed the Cherokee syllabary around 1821.

explanation.why: A similarity must say what the two writing systems have in common. The notes show that both Sejong and Sequoyah wanted their people to be able to read and write their own language, and only one choice states this shared purpose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It points out a difference in what the symbols stand for, not a similarity.
explanation.B: Correct. It names the purpose the two writing systems share.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It contrasts the dates of the two systems, which is a difference.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes only the Cherokee syllabary, so it cannot show what the two systems have in common.
